title: Peter and Paul in Rome (c. 64–67)
hookLine: tradition holds Peter was crucified upside down and Paul beheaded under Nero

lines: YOU WILL STRETCH OUT YOUR HANDS.
cards: By the Sea of Tiberias, after a breakfast of bread and fish, the risen Jesus tells Peter how his life will end. When you were younger, he says, you dressed yourself and walked where you liked.
When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will dress you and lead you where you would not go. John adds one quiet line: this was to show by what death Peter would glorify God.
Then the Bible goes silent. Where Peter's road ends, and Paul's, is told by the generations after.

teach.b: Start with Paul. In the Second Letter to Timothy, Paul writes as a prisoner to a younger friend, in the Douay-Rheims: "I have fought a good fight, I have finished my course, I have kept the faith."
A few lines later he asks Timothy to hurry before winter, and bring the cloak he left behind, and his books. A man who knows the end is close. Now the tradition.
Early Christian writers, collected by the historian Eusebius, say both apostles died in Rome under the emperor Nero. Tradition says Paul, a Roman citizen as Acts tells us, was beheaded.
And it says Peter was crucified, and asked to hang head downward, because he did not think himself worthy to die the way his Lord had.
That detail comes from writings outside the Bible; Catholics hold it as tradition, not scripture. Now the names.
In Matthew's Gospel Jesus gives Simon a new one: "thou art Peter; and upon this rock I will build my church."
Catholics see the bishops of Rome as Peter's successors, and Saint Peter's Basilica stands over the place tradition names as his grave.
The tentmaker: Acts says Paul made tents with his hands, and Paul writes that he labored night and day so as not to be a burden.
A fisherman and a craftsman, and not always at peace: Paul says he opposed Peter to his face in Antioch over who could eat with whom.
Yet the Church keeps their feast together, on one day.

teach.h: UPON THIS ROCK I WILL BUILD MY CHURCH.
teach.b: Some paintings set them side by side, Peter with the keys, Paul with the sword that tradition says took his head, and between them a quarrel neither the Bible nor the Church ever hid.

how: Catholics keep one shared feast for Saints Peter and Paul, pray at the tombs tradition names as theirs in Rome, and pray for persecuted Christians at Mass and in their own prayers.

games.q: you're Paul at Antioch. Peter used to eat with gentile Christians, but now he has stopped, afraid of what others will say. what do you do?
o: say nothing, to keep the peace.
leave and start your own church.
games.why: Paul says he withstood Peter to the face, because it wasn't right. the Church still keeps them together on one feast.

practice: Remember Christians who suffer for their faith today. You don't need names: just someone, somewhere, who will go to Mass this week knowing it could cost them a job, a home, their safety.
If you pray, ask for their courage and protection, and for the people who threaten them; if you don't, keep them in mind.

wordCard.voice: Cephas. The Aramaic name John also gives Simon Peter, alongside the Greek Petros, rock. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek: Peter — in Matthew 16:18 the name sits beside petra, rock. John gives the Aramaic too: Cephas.

carryVoice: Your line: the rock and the tentmaker. Two very different men, one feast. See you tomorrow.
